common_name: Stansfieldii Hens and Chicks (Flat-Topped Cobweb Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Stansfieldii is a distinctive selection of cobweb houseleek with flattened, unusually broad rosettes in green flushed red, knit together by the fine white webbing typical of the arachnoideum group. Press small offsets onto the surface of lean, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun, where the webbing and red tones develop most fully. It multiplies quickly into a dense mat of tightly packed rosettes and tolerates being crowded, though older centers benefit from occasional thinning to keep the webbing visible. As with other cobweb sempervivums, it is intolerant of standing water and performs best in a rock garden, trough, or raised bed with excellent drainage.
sources: British Cactus and Succulent Society reference

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Named for the English alpine nursery where it was raised, Rocknoll Rosette is grown for the way its evergreen rosettes shift color through the seasons, holding an olive-green base in winter and flushing deep red and gold once summer sun intensifies. The truncated, slightly blunted leaf tips give the rosette a tidy, compact look distinct from more pointed sempervivum types. Plant offsets in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun, which is essential for bringing out the strongest color contrast, and allow the mat to spread by its own short-stemmed offsets. It is fully cold hardy and needs no winter protection where drainage is good.

common_name: Hausmanii Hens and Chicks (Purple-Tipped Velvety Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: A historic hybrid between Sempervivum arachnoideum and S. montanum, Hausmanii forms medium-sized rosettes clothed in a soft, velvety fuzz over plush green leaves that narrow to sharply pointed, wine-purple tips. That combination of fine hairs and dark points gives the plant a distinctly shaggy, two-toned look compared with smoother-leaved cultivars. Grow in lean, mineral soil in full sun, where the tip color deepens and the rosettes stay compact; part shade produces looser, greener growth. It offsets readily on short stolons and is fully winter hardy in a well-drained rock garden or trough.

common_name: Berry Blues Hens and Chicks (Chick Charms Silvery Blue-Pink Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Berry Blues belongs to Chris Hansen's Chick Charms breeding line and stands out among sempervivums for its powdery, silvery-blue leaf color, which flushes rosy pink to burgundy as temperatures cool in fall and winter. Rosettes stay tight and symmetrical at around four inches across, forming a slow-spreading colony of hens and offset chicks. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to develop the deepest color, since shade fades the blue-gray tones toward plain green. A thick central flowering stalk with starry pink blooms appears occasionally on mature rosettes in summer, after which that particular rosette declines while offsets carry the clump forward.

common_name: Borisii Hens and Chicks (Dense Pale Green Fuzzy Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: One of the older named sempervivums still widely grown today, Borisii forms very dense, small rosettes of pale green leaves covered in a fine fuzz that gives the whole plant a soft, matte texture rather than the glossy look of many cultivars. Mature clumps bear star-shaped greenish-yellow flowers on short stalks in summer, though the tight rosettes are the main attraction. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun, where it multiplies briskly into a low, carpet-like mat well suited to crevices and trough gardens. It tolerates poor, rocky soil far better than rich garden beds and needs no winter protection in cold climates as long as its roots stay dry.

common_name: Lilac Time Hens and Chicks (Blue-Gray Rosette Turning Lilac)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: Bred in England in the early 1980s, Lilac Time produces unusually large rosettes that open blue-gray and take on a soft lilac-pink cast under strong summer sun, then deepen toward red-bronze once cold weather sets in. The size and pastel coloring make it stand out in mixed sempervivum plantings dominated by smaller, more uniformly red or green cultivars. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to bring out the lilac tones, since shaded plants stay a duller gray-green. Established clumps send up pink, star-shaped flower spikes in summer and offset steadily to form a broad, slow-spreading colony.
sources: British Cactus and Succulent Society reference

common_name: Pacific Devil's Food Hens and Chicks (Large Chocolate-Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of lean, sharply drained gravelly soil in full sun in spring or fall.

directions: A Gosset-bred selection from the Pacific series of Washington state hybridizers, Pacific Devil's Food is grown for its large rosettes, which run five or six inches across at maturity and hold rich red tones nearly all year, deepening toward chocolate-purple in cold weather and warming toward gold-red in summer. It offsets prolifically, quickly building a colony a foot or more across from a single starting rosette. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to maximize both size and color saturation, since shaded plants stay smaller and greener. Its vigor and reliable color make it a popular anchor plant for mixed sempervivum troughs and rock gardens.

common_name: Blushing Beauty Aeonium (Pale Green Red-Tinged Aeonium)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in full sun to light shade for the strongest blush color.

directions: Bred by California hybridizer Jack Catlin from a cross of Aeonium canariense and the dark-leaved Zwartkop, Blushing Beauty carries pale green rosettes edged and washed in soft coral-red, with the blush intensifying under the mild stress of bright sun and dry soil. It grows on branching stems that slowly build a small, open shrub rather than staying flat like its canariense parent. Plant in gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot inland gardens, since too much shade fades the color to plain green while extreme heat can bleach it. Water during the cool-season active growth period and let the soil dry out in summer dormancy, when the plant is most vulnerable to rot.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in full sun to light shade for the deepest plum color.

directions: Another Jack Catlin hybrid from Zwartkop crossed with Aeonium canariense, Plum Purdy opens each new leaf bright green before it rapidly darkens to a rich plum-purple, so mature rosettes often show a lighter green heart ringed by deep purple outer leaves. The two-tone effect is most pronounced on actively growing plants in strong sun. Grow in fast-draining gritty soil in full sun to light shade, watering through the cool growing season and withholding water during summer dormancy to prevent stem rot. Older plants branch from the base into a multi-headed clump and can be kept compact by pinching or propagated easily from stem cuttings.

common_name: Zwartkin Aeonium (Compact Flat Dark Disc Rosette)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in full sun for the darkest, flattest rosette form.

directions: Zwartkin combines the near-black foliage of Aeonium arboreum 'Zwartkop' with the low, flattened, disc-like rosette shape of Aeonium tabuliforme, producing a compact hybrid that stays closer to the ground than either full-size tree aeoniums or the true saucer plant. Leaves darken from green toward deep maroon-black as they mature and as sun exposure increases, giving the rosette a striking two-toned look before it fully colors up. Grow in gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun, watering during the cool growing season and keeping the soil nearly dry through summer dormancy. It branches and offsets at the base over time, and its compact habit suits container culture better than larger black-leaved aeoniums.

common_name: Sun Dancer Aeonium (Cream-Margined Variegated Green Rosette)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in bright light to keep the variegated margins crisp.

directions: Patented by Altman Plants breeder Renee O'Connell, Sun Dancer forms even, concentric rosettes of green leaves bordered in creamy white, creating a geometric variegated pattern that reads almost like a pinwheel from above. Unlike many slower variegated succulents, it offsets freely from an early age, quickly forming a cluster of same-size rosettes rather than a single dominant head. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in bright light, since the sharpest cream margins develop under strong sun while still keeping the plant frost-free. Water during the cool active-growth season and reduce watering in summer, and separate rooted offsets to propagate true-to-type divisions.

common_name: Cala Gasteria (Compact Chunky Dark Rosette Form)

planting.note: Pot offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or open shade; suitable outdoors in zone 9-11 or as a low-light houseplant elsewhere.

directions: Named for the Cala Pass area of South Africa's Eastern Cape where it grows on cliffs, this compact form of Gasteria excelsa forms unusually chunky, thick rosettes that darken from deep green to nearly black when exposed to more light, unlike the typically taller and paler species. Grow in a shallow pot of gritty, mineral succulent mix in bright indirect light or open shade, moving plants gradually into stronger light to build up dark coloration without scorching the leaves. It clumps slowly from basal offsets rather than spreading rapidly, staying tidy for years in a small container. Water only once the mix has dried fully, since like most gasterias it is far more likely to suffer from overwatering than drought.

planting.note: Pot offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or open shade; suitable outdoors in zone 9-11 or as a low-light houseplant elsewhere.

directions: Collected near Stutterheim in South Africa's Eastern Cape, Gaika is a paler, more strongly striped form of Gasteria excelsa, its long tongue-shaped leaves marked with lengthwise light and dark banding rather than the more even green tone of typical excelsa. Grow in a wide, shallow pot of gritty mineral succulent mix in bright indirect light, which keeps the striping crisp without bleaching the leaves. It forms a slow-growing rosette that eventually clumps into a small colony of offsets, and mature plants send up tall, arching flower spikes lined with tubular pink-and-green blooms in spring. Keep soil on the dry side and let the mix dry out fully between waterings to avoid basal rot.

planting.note: Pot offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or open shade; suitable outdoors in zone 9-11 or as a low-light houseplant elsewhere.

directions: This wild-collected form of Gasteria excelsa is named for the locality where it grows clinging to dry stone walls and cliff faces, and it is distinguished by unusually long, curved leaves that taper to sharp, scimitar-like points rather than the blunter tips typical of the species. Grow in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light or open shade, siting it where the long leaves have room to arch outward without being brushed against. It is slow to clump but produces a striking, architectural rosette as it matures, and tolerates lower light than most succulents, making it useful for shaded patios or bright rooms. Water sparingly, letting the mix dry completely between waterings.

common_name: Winter Red Pig's Ear (Paddle-Leaf Red-Margined Cotyledon)

planting.note: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; the powdery leaf coating rubs off easily, so handle transplants gently.

directions: Winter Red is a widely offered pig's ear selection whose chalky, powder-white leaves run slightly longer and narrower than the typical rounded species, tapering to a paddle-like shape edged in bright red where the plant gets full sun. The red margin is most vivid on plants grown lean and bright, fading toward plain gray-green if kept in too much shade or overly rich soil. Long, bell-shaped red flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage in winter, giving the cultivar its name and providing color when most succulents are dormant. Plant in fast-draining, mineral soil in full sun to very light shade, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings allowed to callus before rooting.

common_name: Elk Horns Pig's Ear (Multi-Pronged Silver-White Cotyledon)

planting.note: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; the powdery leaf coating rubs off easily, so handle transplants gently.

directions: Elk Horns takes its name from the way each leaf, though rounded and powdery silver-white as it emerges, gradually flattens and splits into two or three antler-like prongs as it matures, a habit unlike the simple oval leaves of the typical species. Leaf tips are often finely edged in crimson, standing out sharply against the pale, chalky leaf surface. In late spring and early summer, tall flower stalks carry drooping, bell-shaped blooms ranging from yellow to orange-red well above the foliage. Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, and avoid handling or overhead watering that would wipe off the protective powdery coating; propagate from stem or leaf cuttings that have callused for a few days.

common_name: Happy Young Lady Pig's Ear (Upright Finger-Leaf Cotyledon)

planting.note: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; the powdery leaf coating rubs off easily, so handle transplants gently.

directions: Happy Young Lady grows as an upright, stemmed succulent with long, slender, finger-like leaves reaching skyward rather than sprawling outward, each coated in the powdery white farina typical of the species and blushed red at the tips under bright light. The narrow, elongated leaf form makes it look noticeably more slender and vertical than rounder pig's ear cultivars grown alongside it. Showy coral-orange, bell-shaped flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage, typically in fall. Grow in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun to very light shade, and stake or support taller stems if they begin to lean; propagate by rooting stem cuttings after a short callusing period.
